emergency.title: Get emergency care now
emergency.body: What you told us can be serious. Call an ambulance, or go to the nearest hospital emergency department now.
emergency.source: Arogya Kavacha 108, National Health Mission Karnataka

selfharm.title: Please talk to someone now
selfharm.body: What you are feeling matters, and you don't have to carry it alone. Tele-MANAS is a free government helpline, open day and night.
selfharm.source: Tele-MANAS, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

unsafe.title: If you are not safe where you are
unsafe.body: If you can, move to a place with other people around. The Women Helpline can connect you to a One Stop Centre for shelter, police, legal and medical help.
unsafe.source: One Stop Centre scheme (Sakhi), Ministry of Women and Child Development

pep.title: Ask for medicine to prevent HIV (PEP)
pep.body: PEP can stop HIV from taking hold after forced or unprotected sex. It must be started within 72 hours, and it works best the sooner it starts. A doctor decides if you need it and tells you how to take it. It is free at government hospitals and ART centres.

ec.title: If pregnancy is possible, get emergency contraception
ec.body: Emergency contraception pills work better the sooner you take them. They are sold at pharmacies without a prescription. A doctor can also fit a copper IUD, which can work for up to 5 days after.
ec.source: MoHFW 2014 medico-legal guidelines; WHO emergency contraception fact sheet

cantgo.title: If you can't get to a hospital right now
points: PEP cannot be started at home. Only a doctor can give it. You still have time: it can be started up to 72 hours after, so try to go today or tomorrow.
Call 1097, the free National AIDS Helpline, to ask where PEP is available near you.
If you have no way to travel, call 108 for a free ambulance, or 181 for the Women Helpline.
Emergency contraception pills are sold at pharmacies without a prescription. Ask the pharmacist how to take them.
If you may want to file a complaint later, try not to wash, and keep the clothes you were wearing in a paper bag. This is your choice. Getting care comes first.
cantgo.source: NACO helpline 1097; Arogya Kavacha 108; MoHFW 2014 medico-legal guidelines

drugged.title: If you think you were drugged
drugged.body: Tell the doctor as soon as you can. Some drugs leave the body within hours, so tests work best early. Avoid alcohol and any medicine you were not given by a doctor until you are checked.

injury.title: Get your injuries checked
injury.body: Even if they seem small. Some injuries don't show on the outside. For survivors of assault, treatment is free at any hospital.

pepLate.title: The time for PEP has probably passed
pepLate.body: PEP has to be started within 72 hours. You can still get tested for HIV and other infections, and get treatment if you need it.

ecLate.title: If you might be pregnant, see a doctor soon
ecLate.body: A copper IUD may still work up to 5 days after. After that, a doctor can explain what choices you have.

sti.title: Get checked for infections
sti.body: A doctor can give medicine to prevent some infections, and treat pain, burning, discharge or sores. Some tests are more accurate a few weeks later, so the doctor may ask you to come back.

pregnancy.title: Take a pregnancy test
pregnancy.body: Pregnancy tests are sold at pharmacies and are available at government health centres. If the test is positive, a doctor can explain your choices.

under18.title: If you are under 18
under18.body: You will still get free treatment. Different rules apply, and the hospital must inform the police. Childline can help you.

complaint.title: If you want to file a complaint
complaint.body: You can complain at any police station, even if it happened somewhere else. You don't have to decide today. The hospital will inform the police, but your treatment does not depend on you filing a complaint.

talk.title: Talk to someone
talk.body: What happened is not your fault. Free counselling and support are available at One Stop Centres and on the phone.

authority.title: If the person was police or someone with power
authority.body: You can still complain, and you do not have to go to the station where this person works. You can go to any police station (Zero FIR), or send your complaint in writing to a senior police officer. The Women Helpline or a One Stop Centre can help you and go with you.
authority.source: BNSS 2023, Section 173 (Zero FIR; complaint to the Superintendent of Police); One Stop Centre scheme

general.title: See a doctor
general.body: You can show them what you wrote. You don't have to say anything about your work.

pep.name: Medicine to prevent HIV (PEP)
pep.say: “I need PEP. It happened in the last 3 days.”

sti.name: Infection tests and treatment
sti.say: “I want to be tested for infections.”

counselling.name: Someone to talk to
counselling.say: “I'd like to talk to a counsellor.”

checkup.name: Regular health check-up
checkup.say: “I'd like a health check-up and infection tests.”
checkup.note: You don't need to say anything about your work.

rights.title: Free treatment at any hospital
rights.body: Government and private hospitals must give first aid and treatment to survivors of sexual assault, free of cost.

rights.title: The hospital will inform the police
rights.body: The law requires hospitals to tell the police. Getting treatment does not depend on you filing a complaint.

rights.title: Your consent comes first
rights.body: A doctor must ask before any examination. You can say no to any part of it.

rights.title: Complain at any police station
rights.body: You can file a complaint at any police station, even if it happened somewhere else.

rights.title: No two-finger test
rights.body: This test is banned. No one can do it to you.
rights.source: Supreme Court of India; MoHFW 2014 guidelines

rights.title: If you are under 18
rights.body: Treatment is still free. Different rules apply, and the hospital must inform the police.
